data.title: Visegrád – another Great Moravian hillfort in Hungary (HU)
data.excerpt: Visegrád in Hungary, about 7 km as the crow flies from Štúrovo, is best known for its royal upper castle, built only after the Mongol invasion. Far fewer people know that on the neighbouring lower hill stands an older, originally Roman fort which the Slavs of Great Moravia turned into an important hillfort and local administrative centre, and which they named Vyšehrad – the high castle.
data.metaTitle: Visegrád – a Great Moravian hillfort on a Roman fort
data.metaDescription: At Visegrád in Hungary the Slavs of Great Moravia reused an older Roman fort as an administrative centre; a royal castle rose here only much later.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: About 7 km as the crow flies from Štúrovo, on Šibrikov kopec (the lower neighbouring hill opposite today's upper castle)

keyFacts.label: The Roman fort of Pone Navata
keyFacts.value: Triangular ground plan, dimensions c. 130 × 140 m, part of the Limes Romanus; abandoned in the 5th century

keyFacts.label: The Slavic Vyšehrad
keyFacts.value: The name means “high castle” — documented in written sources as early as 1009; a local administrative centre of the Nitra part of Great Moravia

keyFacts.label: Pre-Romanesque church
keyFacts.value: Foundations of the 10th century, beneath them an 8th-century spur and a wattle wall from the turn of the 8th/9th centuries

keyFacts.label: The count's seat
keyFacts.value: A stone building of the early 11th century on the ruins of Roman structures, 16.5 × 10/9 m, with a heated room

keyFacts.label: The prison of King Solomon
keyFacts.value: In 1081 the deposed King Solomon was imprisoned here on the orders of St Ladislaus

keyFacts.label: Today
keyFacts.value: The museum at Visegrád displays finds typical of the Great Moravian period, although Hungarian literature barely mentions the Slavic hillfort

timeline.description: King Andrew I had a monastery of the Eastern rite built for the monks who came with his wife Anastasia from Kiev — before he began building the abbey at Tihany.

timeline.title: The provostry church and Solomon's imprisonment
timeline.description: After 1063 a sumptuous provostry church with frescoes was built; in 1081 St Ladislaus had the deposed King Solomon shut up in a tower of the fort.

timeline.title: Changes in the monastery's administration
timeline.description: The Orthodox monastery was taken over by the Benedictines in the 1220s and later, in 1490, by the Paulines.

timeline.title: Decline of the county centre
timeline.description: Like other county seats without an advantageous economic position, Visegrád too began to decline to the level of a village market centre.

timeline.title: Demise of the county castle
timeline.description: The neglected county castle on Šibrikov kopec fell victim to the Mongols; after their departure it was never restored.

timeline.title: Demise of the monastery
timeline.description: The Orthodox monastery disappeared completely during Turkish rule.

timeline.title: Construction of the new upper and lower castle
timeline.description: As part of Béla IV's programme, today's upper castle of Visegrád and the lower castle (Solomon's Tower) were built; stones from the abandoned county castle were reused.

children.text: Visegrád lies in Hungary about 7 km as the crow flies from Štúrovo. It is a whole complex of monuments, of which the best known today is the royal castle built only after the Mongol invasion on the highest hill in the area – the so-called upper castle, in which the Hungarian coronation jewels were also kept for a time. At the foot of this hill lie, on the one hand, the lower castle with Solomon's Tower, which controlled the road beside the Danube, and on the other the sumptuous Renaissance royal palace. Few people, however, know of the older, originally Roman fort on the adjacent lower hill, which even before the arrival of the Old Hungarians was used by the Slavs in the time of Great Moravia as an important hillfort – an administrative centre – and which they named Vyšehrad (the high castle).

The original Vyšehrad was built on the so-called Šibrikov kopec (Sibrik Hill) directly above the Danube. In the 4th century the Romans built a fort here in the shape of a triangle enclosed by an outer wall. The walls were protected by numerous towers, and in 372 a larger watchtower was also built. The fort evidently formed part of the northern defences of the Roman Empire – the Limes Romanus. The Roman fort was built at the end of the 320s, has an irregular ground plan, and the length of its sides is around 130 × 140 m. According to the Notitia Dignitatum the name of the fort was Pone Navata. The Roman guards abandoned the fort in the 5th century.

children.text: In the 9th century the Slavs used the remains of the Roman fortification and built a hillfort on Šibrikov kopec. Among other things, Vyšehrad controlled both the river and the overland routes in the Danube gorge, as well as the surrounding fords, but above all it served as a local administrative centre, one of the centres of the territorial districts into which Great Moravia was organisationally divided. These territorial units, which were part of the Nitra portion of Great Moravia, evidently continued earlier tribal and also supra-tribal formations that had been taking shape at least since the turn of the 8th and 9th centuries, and in the course of the existence of the Great Moravian state they gradually developed into castle districts – ispánates. So far, however, I have not managed to find out whether the Slavs merely occupied the originally Roman fort (which in the time of Great Moravia had already been abandoned by the Roman garrison for several centuries, so that it may be assumed to have been considerably dilapidated) and only repaired it, or whether they built a typical Slavic timber-and-earth fortification on its site.

In 2013 Hungarian archaeologists carried out new excavations at Visegrád, the results of which they summarised in an article in the journal Hungarian Archeology in 2014. In it they also give data that relate directly to the Slavic occupation of Šibrik. Among other things, they mention the foundations of a pre-Romanesque church, which they date to the 10th century. Beneath the foundations of the church an 8th-century spur was found, and also the remains of a wattle wall dated to the turn of the 8th and 9th centuries. 
 
 Further, on the outer side of the church a grave was found which respects the walls of the church and in which a priest is probably buried. Among other interesting things, part of a chalice was found in his grave. The Hungarians again date this grave to the 10th century, or at the latest to the beginning of the 11th century. I think, however, that it cannot be ruled out that the church, as well as the grave, may be dated to the period of Great Moravia. 
 
 In the article they go on to write that "The undoubtedly Slavic name of the place (the name Visegrad documented in written sources as early as 1009), in combination with the new results of the research, may serve as a basis for determining the ethnicity of the inhabitants who gave the fort its name. Thus, in this light, a continuous occupation by the original Slavic population up to the early Árpád period may be assumed."

children.text: After the emergence of the Kingdom of Hungary in the time of King Stephen I, Visegrád did not lose its importance and became the seat of a county. Visegrád is mentioned as a county seat for the first time in 1009, in a charter of King Stephen. This charter states that part of the bishop's ecclesiastical area
(I do not know what term to use here, I am no expert – translator's note)

is also “Visegrád civitas” (civitas means city, but this text interprets it here as a county...). Visegrád county (like Esztergom county lying further upstream and Fejér (White) county further downstream) covered the adjoining area on both banks of the Danube. Visegrád is one of the proofs that the newly emerging Hungarian state took over its administrative division directly from the Great Moravian Empire. At the same time it is one of the arguments for the claim that the originally Moravian, or Nitran, nobility must also have played a significant part in the emergence of the Kingdom of Hungary, since it could have ensured the continuity of state administration and of the administrative division of the newly emerging state.

children.text: In the south-eastern part of the castle, excavations uncovered the foundations of a larger stone building of the early 11th century, built on the ruins of structures from Roman times; it was probably the seat of the count. Dimensions: length 16.5 m, width 10 or 9 m; inside, the building was divided by a wall into 2 rooms. The eastern room was heated by a stone stove.

An interesting piece of information is given by the Hungarian historians SZŐKE Mátyás and Györffy, according to whom King Andrew I had an Orthodox monastery (of the Eastern rite) built at Visegrád, in the valley below Šibrikov kopec (even before he began the construction of the abbey at Tihany –
the Benedictine monastery there was founded in 1055, translator's note
. He evidently founded the monastery of the Eastern rite for “Greek” monks (
who knows whether Greek, perhaps Slavic as well!!!)

, who came with his wife Anastasia from Kiev. This monastery was taken over by the Benedictines in the 1220s, and later, in a rather neglected state, by the Paulines in 1490. During Turkish rule, around 1560, it disappeared completely. After archaeological investigation we now know its ground plan; there is some sort of convalescent home there now.
It is remarkable that Andrew I had this “Slavic monastery” built in a place where Slavs also lived.

During the struggles for the crown in 1081, (King) St Ladislaus had the overthrown King Solomon shut up in one of the towers of this fort. At that time today's Solomon's Tower in the lower castle of Visegrád did not yet exist. Today, after 900 years, it is difficult to determine in which part of the castle that prison was. It is also hard to find an explanation for why the royal prisoner was held precisely at this castle. Perhaps a role is played here by the fact that at that time Dömös was the seat of the Danubian estates of the Béla branch of the Árpáds, while nearby Visegrád was the seat of the Andrew branch. Solomon was thus held captive at his “own” castle. After 1063, on the site of the first church, a sumptuous main provostry church decorated with period frescoes was built.

Like the other county seats that did not have an advantageous geographical and economic position, the Visegrád centre too began to decline in the 12th century. The counts did not take much care of them, staying mainly on their own estates or near the king. The county seats slowly sank to the level of village market centres, and the neglected county castles became easy prey for the Mongols in the 13th century.

children.text: After their departure the county castle on Šibrikov kopec was never restored; instead, today's upper castle of Visegrád was built on the high hill and the lower castle (Solomon's Tower) not far from the old hillfort – all of it as part of Béla IV's castle-building programme after the Mongol invasion.

The original Visegrád did not live to see restoration after the Mongol devastation, because instead of it the construction was begun both of a modern hilltop castle and of the lower castle above the road near Šibrikov kopec. The ruined building stones from the county castle were also carried off and used for the residential tower and the walls of the lower castle.

As can be seen, the Slavic hillfort is indeed mentioned in Hungarian literature, but you will not read anything more detailed about it, despite the fact that excavations were carried out there and that in the museum at Visegrád it is possible to see several finds typical of the period of Great Moravia. Unfortunately, this is a typical phenomenon among our southern neighbours – as if they were closing their eyes to that part of history which does not suit them very much. If anyone has an article or a specialist text relating directly to the hillfort (finds, the construction of the defensive wall, buildings and so on), I will be very grateful if they send it to me at my e-mail address.
